extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and reporters learning how to write event/feature news
extracted.subtask_description: Producing descriptive, human-interest newspaper pieces that report on public events, entertainments, charitable activities, and ceremonies, using scene-setting, quotations, participant lists, and emotional detail to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid scene-setting and concrete details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete, sensory details to establish the scene (e.g., "Flags were hung out of windows all along the Drive," "The arc lights in the park had been turned off...", "It touched the ceiling, and its boughs hung down with its heavy burdens.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide visual, auditory and tactile impressions so readers can picture the event; include specific props, lighting, weather, and physical surroundings as seen in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest anecdotes and direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short, telling anecdotes and direct quotes that reveal character and emotion (e.g., George Sebech: "I am 98 years old, but I'll be marching here ten years from now..."; children's dialogue in the hospital: "I gotta chu-chu... An', an', I gotta dawg.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief, colorful quotes and small stories to personalize the event and create emotional connection; place such anecdotes early or at emotional high points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify participants with names and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: List names, titles and organizations of key participants and officials (e.g., lists of Grand Army staff, Rear Admirals and Generals, chairs of charitable societies, performers and booth attendants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit organizers, officials and notable attendees explicitly; full names and institutional affiliations lend authority and documentary value to the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and report numerical specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Give numbers and counts where relevant (e.g., "thousands and thousands of American flags," "2,000 names on the list to receive presents," "Almas Temple ... is to give away 600 Christmas baskets").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include counts, lists and totals to convey scale and impact; numbers should be used to substantiate claims about size or reach of an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe organizational and logistical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report how the event is organized and runs (e.g., vehicle substitution: "The motor truck has taken the place of the sleigh," Y.W.C.A. hours: "the building ... will be open from 3 until 9 o'clock", plans for distribution and volunteer roles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey practical aspects—who does what, when and where—so readers understand the operation behind the spectacle and know how to participate or benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey audience reaction and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Note crowd response and mood (e.g., "Receiving cheers and shouts of encouragement...", "The crowd of about 2,500... became still.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report applause, silence, cheering, or other reactions to indicate reception and social significance; couple reactions with brief explanation when useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative sequencing of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the sequence of events clearly (parade order: mounted police, battalion, First Division, survivors; pantomime progression: seven gifts, scenes of Pierrot and the Moon Lady).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize event copy so readers can follow the order of presentation; use chronological or logical ordering to structure the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight emotional or moral lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame episodes to show emotional resonance or moral uplift (e.g., the Humble Woman setting her bird free, the Dear Child's worn doll being 'worth all the others'; children's resilience in hospital performances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw out the human or moral significance of small incidents to provide the feature's emotional core without melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe production and technical elements for performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Report staging and production details in theatre/event coverage (e.g., concealed lights, chimes, placards announcing action, music and instrumentation, crowding and sight limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include technical aspects that affected presentation and audience experience—lighting, sound, signage, staging—so readers understand how the show was put together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit charitable and civic organizations and volunteers
rubrics_metrics.description: Name charities, missions, societies and volunteer groups and describe their roles (e.g., Salvation Army, Central Union Mission, Associated Charities, Boy Scouts assisting distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide organizational attribution and note volunteer contributions to acknowledge community effort and provide accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evocative, humanizing style and local color
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ playful, descriptive language and local color in feature writing (examples: humorous obituary of 'Straw Hatt', descriptive costume detail at a lawn fete, Mr. Carnegie 'rolled all the cakes... into one big doughnut').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a voice that fits the feature: witty, compassionate or lyrical as appropriate; specific, colorful details make copy memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the vulnerable or marginalized for sympathy features
rubrics_metrics.description: Center stories on vulnerable populations (crippled schoolchildren, hospital patients, inmates) and show how events benefit or uplift them, with specific scenes and caregivers named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subjects respectfully, emphasize dignity and recovery or joy, include caregivers and program details to show support structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance descriptive detail with succinct reporting of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine rich description and anecdotes with concise facts (times, places, participant lists, outcomes) so the piece is both engaging and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting picturesque detail obscure essential information; ensure lead facts (who/what/when/where/why/how) are present even in feature copy.
